To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the dependability as a predictor of either the presence (Experiment I) or the absence (Experiment II) of shock is important.

rats choose a signalled shock over an unsignailed shock condition when the signal is dependable as a predictor of the presence of shock, but not when it is dependable as a prediction of the absence of shock.

rats choose to receive shocks in a signalled condition if the dependability of signals predicting the presence of shocks is low, and they choose to avoid shocks in a signelled condition if the dependably of signals predicting the absence of shocks is low.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of what controls choice between a signalled and an unsignalled shock condition.
the role of choice and the role of the dependability of signals in the control of behaviour by stimuli.
choice and the dependability as predictors of stimuli that signal either the presence or absence of shock
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the choice of a signalled over an unsignailed condition depends on a stimulus that predicts either the absence or the presence of shock, but that the dependability with which the stimulus predicts the absence of a shock is more important than its dependability as a predictor of the presence of shock.
a stimulus signalling the absence of shock must be a dependable predictor of safety in order for rats to change from an unconditioned to a signalled shock situation.

the dependability or probability of a stimulus predicting either the presence or absence of shock is not a critical variable in determining the probability of changing to a signalled shock or safety condition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the dependability with which a stimulus predicts shock is important in determining whether or not a rat will change from an unsignalled to a signalled shock situation, but the dependability with with a stimulus predicts safety is not important.

the dependability (reliability, validity) of stimuli as predictors of the presence of shock is uncontrolled, but the dependability of predictors of the absence of shock may be important in determining the choice of a signalled condition.
choice is controlled by a signal predicting the presence of shock, but that the dependability (probability) of the signal as such a predictor is not important.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dependability (reliability) of a stimulus that predicts shock is not important in controlling choice.
the stimulus that predicts the safety of the environment is more important than the stimulus that predicts shock.

rats are willing to change to the signalled shock condition, even when the dependability (or reliability) of the signal as either a predictor of shock or a predictor of the absence of shock has been degraded.
